anomaly_def.Name: Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly : Simultaneous transactions hold or request mutually incompatible locks on the same data items, creating long blocking chains or deadlocks inside the lock-manager layer and stalling statement execution. 
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : The database process or its children hit kernel-enforced ceilings for file descriptors, shared memory, semaphores, threads, or other OS-level objects, preventing creation of new backends, workers, or I/O contexts. 
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Server- or network-side constraints on sockets, listener backlogs, authentication threads, or transport capacity limit the establishment and servicing of client connections.

When these three root causes co-exist, the system exhibits a blended failure pattern: existing sessions become trapped in prolonged lock waits or cyclical deadlocks while new clients experience connection refusals, timeouts, or prolonged authentication delays. Lock-bound backends that cannot complete free their locks slowly or hold them indefinitely if OS limits block their ability to write to WAL, open extra files, or spawn background workers; this prolongs blocking chains and inflates wait-event and deadlock counters. Concurrently, exhausted file-handle or thread quotas reduce the pool of accept()able sockets, so the listener queues overflow, causing TCP resets and application-level connection storms that repeatedly retry and further raise incoming connection pressure. Monitoring shows runaway lock-wait times, rising deadlock victim counts, sharp drops in completed transactions per second, escalating OS error messages about "too many open files" or "cannot create thread", and surges in half-open sockets and retransmissions.

Causally, heavy lock contention increases backend counts and prolongs session lifetimes, accelerating consumption of OS resources (descriptors, semaphores, threads). Once kernel limits are hit, the database cannot create additional server processes or worker threads, which in turn prevents deadlock detectors, autovacuum workers, or I/O helpers from starting, delaying lock resolution and log flushing and deepening the backlog. Simultaneously, socket and backlog exhaustion triggered by the same OS limits or by retry storms prevents blocked applications from reconnecting to roll back or retry, leaving their orphaned transactions and locks in limbo. The feedback loop between in-engine lock stalls, OS-level exhaustion, and network-layer connection failures amplifies service degradation, potentially leading to a full outage even though each individual anomaly might have been survivable on its own.

entry.official_definition: Terminates any session that has been idle within an open transaction for longer than the specified amount of time.
entry.trigger_condition: A session is idle, waiting for a client query, while an open transaction remains active longer than the configured threshold.
entry.workload_impact: The session is terminated; this prevents long idle transactions from holding locks or preventing vacuum cleanup.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
